..(Thursday night through Tuesday)
Issued at 552 AM EDT Wed Oct 21 2026

Ridging remains the dominant weather feature for the majority of the 
long term forecast period, leading to seasonably tranquil sensible 
weather in Eastern Kentucky for the foreseeable future. The forecast 
guidance suite is in remarkably good agreement through early next 
week; it collectively resolves an amplified mid/upper level ridge 
stretching up the Mississippi and Ohio River Valleys. The JKL CWA 
will be situated to the east of the ridge axis through Monday, which 
translates to persistent north-northwesterly winds aloft. These 
winds will work to reinforce the dry, continental airmass currently 
in place over the area, as will the synoptic subsidence downstream 
of the ridge axis apex. At the surface, the corresponding (and 
rather broad) high pressure system will remain centered to the 
northeast of the forecast area. The continued influence of that 
anticyclone will keep low level winds light and variable and further 
limit the potential for meaningful airmass modification. Thus, even 
as this ridging pattern begins to break down early next week, the 
antecedent dryness should prevent meaningful precipitation chances 
from materializing.  

Given all of the above, expect efficient diurnal processes to 
dominate the daily forecast. Mostly clear skies will favor plentiful 
solar insolation during the daytime hours, with temperatures warming 
towards highs in the upper half of the 60s/low 70s each day. 
Efficient mixing should yield 20-30 degree dewpoint depressions each 
afternoon/evening, but the light nature of the winds should help 
mitigate any fire weather concerns. As the sun goes down each 
evening, valley locales will begin to thermally decouple. 
Temperatures should quickly drop off in the area's shaded hollows, 
with lows likely bottoming out in the mid 30s within the area's more 
sheltered valleys. Patchy frost cannot be ruled out in these 
conventionally cooler spots, but overnight fog formation is favored 
over frost in the area's broader valleys. The area's rivers, lakes, 
creeks, and streams will provide just enough extra moisture and 
radiative insulation to keep low temperatures closer to the 40 
degree mark in the area's more populated broader valleys. These 
highs and lows are near climatological averages for late October in 
Eastern Kentucky.

As hinted at in the opening paragraph, this ridging pattern is 
progged to break down in the initial stages of the next work week. 
The previously-pronounced ridge axis will retreat to the south of 
the CWA amidst midlevel height falls on Monday, leading to less 
subsidence in the column. As the ridge flattens further on Tuesday, 
the flow aloft will shift towards a west-southwesterly orientation. 
These changes will yield relatively greater amounts of midlevel 
moisture in the column by midweek, and cloud cover should gradually 
increase from Monday night into Tuesday. Model spread begins to 
increase by Wednesday, largely due to differences in the evolution 
of a series of troughs digging into the Upper Midwest around 
midweek. If any of those disturbances digs deep enough to yield more 
vertically continuous southwesterly flow into our CWA, the area 
could see its next round of rain chances. Mentionable PoPs should 
hold off until beyond the end of the official forecast period 
though. LREF ensemble data resolves a less than 10% chance for 
measurable (> 0.01 inches) rainfall through next Wednesday, but 
neighborhood-based ensemble precipitation probabilities increase to 
30% on Thursday. This will give us something to monitor in future 
forecast packages, but in the mean time, the forecast looks 
fantastic for outdoor fall activities. Seasonably cool temperatures, 
light winds, and fair skies will allow fall foliage to reach peak 
color in the coming weeks. This will lead to beautiful scenery 
across Eastern Kentucky, so we encourage readers to get outside and 
enjoy these quintessential autumnal weather conditions!
